additions.english: saqmunya when you need to evacuate bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as halilaj . To correct a dyscrasia that occurs later in those with tumors in the viscera, their diarrhea may weaken them; if you are forced to do so, use things like ivy and safflower for them. As for the purgative and khiyar shanbar , Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that is easily moved to vomit, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring when the time is right." This rids the body of fatigue. Know that if the person drinking it is accustomed to a loose stool or is not accustomed to vomiting, they should avoid it in times when it is not needed. It is necessary to prepare before diarrhea by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages at that time, as this rids the body of fatigue. Know that the one who drinks it—if they are accustomed to a loose stool or are not accustomed to vomiting—should [use] one of the reducing regimens before using a strong medicine. Diarrhea with abdominal flaccidity is difficult and tiring. A purgative medicine may act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, if taken during extreme hunger, or if the person is accustomed to a loose stool, or if the medicine is heavier in essence than in speed of descent. The purgative may remain, causing trouble due to the weakness of the stomach, extreme heaviness, or because the medicine irritates it, or the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested humor, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it throughout the body, dominating the body and attracting other humors to it, increasing that humor in the body. Among the humors, some are quicker to respond to vomiting, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a condition like milk and stars ; its diarrhea is safer in itself. Whoever has a humor flowing downward, such as those with intestinal slippage, the gripping of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. That which is composed of medicines that are strongly different during the time of diarrhea causes the diarrhea to become agitated; the first will purge the second before the second can purge, and perhaps the first will purge the very same second. Whoever is exposed to diarrhea and their body is not cleansed of it, it must be from a drug or colic and distress that befalls them, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, if a medicine evacuates the waste, there will be no agitation with it. If it is taken with agitation, then either it is evacuating what is not waste, or if the evacuated humor changes through vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the purification of the body from the humor intended to be evacuated.
